A second baccalaureate degree may not be attempted until the first has been awarded. A student may complete two majors simultaneously. Matriculation in a second degree will be approved only if:

The student files with the Registrar’s Office a statement of approval by the dean of the college/school and the chair of the department in which she or he wishes to complete the second degree;

The student’s major for the second degree is taken in a subject matter field other than the one in which she or he was awarded the first degree; and furthermore,

The credit-hour requirements for the major leading to the second baccalaureate degree are those specified in the current catalog and will have been earned after the awarding of the first baccalaureate degree.

In addition, the following regulations apply:

A minimum of 32 credit hours toward the second baccalaureate degree must be completed in residence at the University of Guam.

Students holding a baccalaureate degree from other U.S. accredited four-year colleges and universities or foreign equivalent may attempt a second baccalaureate degree at the University of Guam provided they meet the relevant requirements listed above.

In some cases, the General Education requirements may be waived when the student is pursuing a second baccalaureate degree.

The Western Interstate Commission for Higher Education (WICHE) is a regional organization created by the Western Regional Education Compact and adopted in the 1950s by Western states. WICHE was created to facilitate resource sharing among the higher education systems of the West. Helping students gain affordable access to higher education is one of its objectives.

The Western Undergraduate Exchange (WUE) is coordinated by WICHE. Students enrolled through WUE pay up to 150% of the enrolling institution’s resident undergraduate tuition. To qualify, applicants must demonstrate residency in a WICHE member state and must be admitted to a WUE-eligible major at UOG.

WICHE's member states include 15 Western states and member U.S. Pacific Territories and Freely Associated States (currently, the Republic of Marshall Islands, Federated States of Micronesia (FSM), Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, Republic of Paulau and Guam). WICHE’s 15 member states are: Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Hawaii, Idaho, Montana, Nevada, New Mexico, North Dakota, Oregon, South Dakota, Utah, Washington, and Wyoming.

item.content:encoded:
Calvo's Donates $3M to UOG Endowment (Read More)

From UOG to PhD: Alumnus turns passion for human behavior into a career improving workplaces

University of Guam alumnus Nelmar J. Cruz has turned his interest in understanding human behavior into a career helping organizations build better workplaces, support employees, and improve performance.

Cruz, a 2015 UOG graduate with bachelor's degrees in psychology and English literature, earned his doctorate in behavior analysis with an emphasis in organizational behavior management from Florida Tech in spring 2026.

He also earned his master's degree in applied behavior analysis and organizational behavior management from Florida Tech before pursuing his doctorate. He successfully defended his dissertation, titled "A Behavior Analytic Blueprint for Rapport-Building: Investigating the Key Elements for Success," in January.

His doctoral work focuses on organizational behavior management, which applies behavioral principles to improve workplace culture, safety, and performance. Cruz first became a Board-Certified Behavior Analyst (BCBA) in 2019 and earned the doctoral-level designation (BCBA-D) in June 2026.

He currently serves as a business operations specialist at ABA Technologies, where he supports strategic initiatives and organizational improvement. He also teaches part-time in Florida Tech's online behavior analysis master's program.

'Why not make it a better place?' "I help leaders understand what it takes to turn their goals into results. A big part of that is looking at how people work, what influences their performance, and what organizations can do to better support them," Cruz explained.

Cruz helps organizations address challenges involving business performance, employee engagement, and organizational change. Rather than focusing solely on an organization's desired outcomes, he emphasizes understanding what people need to do differently to achieve lasting results.

Cruz's interest in organizational behavior management was largely shaped by his parents, who immigrated to Guam from the Philippines. Growing up, he witnessed how tirelessly they worked to provide for their family. His parents' background, combined with his own experiences working in different settings, motivated Cruz to figure out how workplaces could better support their employees.

"You spend so much time at work, why not make it a better place?" Cruz said

From 'directionless undergrad' to a career with purpose When Cruz first entered UOG, he considered himself a "fairly directionless undergrad," but in time, he found his footing in the psychology program. He became a teaching and behavior lab assistant, as well as a counselor for Isa Psychological Services.

After moving to Florida to pursue his postgraduate studies, he broadened his professional experience by working as a registered behavior technician at a children's autism center before transitioning into roles spanning human resources, organizational capability, project management, and consulting.

Cruz's experiences have ultimately led him to a career that combines his interest in understanding human behavior with his desire to help make workplaces better.

"I want to help organizations and their leaders create the conditions that allow both their business and their people to thrive," he said.

item.description: Calvo's Donates $3M to UOG Endowment (Read More) Tåotao Tritons | Superfan Status: Roland San Nicolas’s Lifelong Loyalty to the San Francisco 49ers
item.content:encoded:
Calvo's Donates $3M to UOG Endowment (Read More)

Tåotao Tritons | Superfan Status: Roland San Nicolas’s Lifelong Loyalty to the San Francisco 49ers

In American football, there are fans—the casual viewers who tune in during game day to cheer on their favorite team. Then, there are superfans—the die-hard followers whose deep devotion extends well beyond the final touchdown at the end of a season. Roland San Nicolas, a librarian and associate professor of library science at the University of Guam, is undoubtedly a superfan. San Nicolas’s love for the San Francisco 49ers is a unique combination of history, family, and an impressive, decades-long memorabilia collection.

“My dad and I watched them play on TV. He was a Niners fan, so I became a Niners fan,” San Nicolas explains of his fanship origins.

That was in 1981, the first year the 49ers won the Super Bowl. They would claim the championship title several more times during San Nicolas’s formative years, quickly establishing themselves as his all-time favorite NFL team.

“They won four times when I was growing up, so it's easy to like a team that's always winning, right?” says San Nicolas.

His loyalty to the red and gold carried on well into adulthood. When his favorite 49ers quarterback, Joe Montana, was traded to the Kansas City Chiefs, San Nicolas continued to follow his career. In college, he had the opportunity to watch Montana in action during a match against the Seattle Seahawks.

An even more memorable event occurred nearly two decades later when San Nicolas finally scored tickets to see the 49ers in person. He watched them on New Year’s Day challenge—and defeat—the Las Vegas Raiders in an electrifying overtime victory. For someone who spent years watching games on TV, seeing the team compete live was a special experience.

When it comes to Niners knowledge, San Nicolas is something of a walking compendium. He can recall important game dates, draft lore, and player statistics, from Hall of Famers like Steve Young and Jerry Rice to modern standouts like Nick Bosa and Brock Purdy.

But San Nicolas just doesn’t remember the greats; he also collects them. He has built a collection of 49ers memorabilia that will amaze even the most hardcore fans.

“Oh, man,” San Nicolas chuckles. “I don't keep a running list because I have thousands of pieces of memorabilia.”

The estimate is not an exaggeration. Whether it’s autographed jerseys, vintage trading cards, small-scale figurines, or everyday items like lanyards, water bottles, and even office supplies, if it has the 49ers logo on it, San Nicolas probably already owns it.

Among his prized pieces are several authentic Joe Montana rookie cards, many of which are professionally appraised to be worth a significant amount of money. The items’ value, however, is less in the price tag and more in the history they represent. San Nicolas also places greater meaning in rare finds that take research and a trained eye to scope out.

“I’m more proud of my pieces that nobody else has instead of stuff that’s mass-produced,” he says.

Meticulous searches through online marketplaces and auctions have yielded some one-of-a-kind pieces, such as an autographed football used by Jerry Rice in a Super Bowl and a voided personal check signed by Joe Montana.

For San Nicolas, these items are snippets of sports history that just can’t be replicated.

Massive memorabilia collection aside, San Nicolas’s connection to the 49ers and football is also highly personal. He played high school football for Father Duenas Memorial School and later for the University of Guam, where he was inducted into the Athletic Hall of Fame in 2023. He played for an outside league as well, earning honors for his time on the field.

Additionally, San Nicolas has instructional experience under his belt. He returned to Father Duenas and coached their football team, helping the Friars secure multiple championship titles throughout his almost 15-year tenure.

San Nicolas continues to pay his love of the game forward at home. Just as his father sparked his passion for football, San Nicolas has done the same with his own children. Both his daughter Iana and son RJ share his allegiance to the Niners, and his son has even gotten into collecting sports memorabilia as well.

The rich array of experiences San Nicolas has amassed throughout the last four decades has only expanded his appreciation for the sport and his go-to team. His distinction as a superfan persists, and there is little doubt that his loyalty to the San Francisco 49ers will waver anytime soon.

item.content:encoded:
Calvo's Donates $3M to UOG Endowment (Read More)

Tåotao Tritons | All the Right Moves: Brionna June Turns Dance into Passion with Purpose

Brionna June is used to being on the move. Before joining the University of Guam as a Senior Retention Specialist, the Atlanta native lived, worked, and studied across the U.S. But no matter where June finds herself, a part of her life that remains constant is dance. The life-long passion has literally kept June on her toes and opened doors to countless opportunities and experiences.

June’s love for dance was built on a foundation of performing that can be traced back to when she was as young as three years old.

“My father’s a pastor, so a lot of the stuff that I did, whether it was singing, dancing, acting, whatever, started in church,” June explains. “I loved performing and being in front of people.”

Wanting her daughter to be well-rounded, June’s mom required her to maintain school grades above 95% and join other sports throughout the year in order to keep dancing. June stayed committed and was able to dance all throughout her K-12 journey and well into college.

Along with joining the marching band dance/flag team at Miles College and earning the position of captain by her sophomore year, June expanded her performance resume considerably. She was a background dancer and singer, joined several stage plays, and had bit parts in some TV shows.

Her time in the spotlight, however, wasn’t meant to last for the long haul.

“When I got older, I realized I wasn’t as prepared for the performance world as I thought I was, so I started tapping into preparing the next generation,” June says, a decision that took her from dancer to choreographer.

After graduating from college, June focused her energy into sharing her skills and knowledge. She began hosting dance clinics for the high schools in her county and fell in love with the impact she could make on up-and-coming dancers.

It was especially important for June to provide the dancers with the guidance she wished she had growing up and to “show them different ways they could be better.” That vision led her to opening her own studio in Atlanta, where teams of young dancers honed their skills in hip hop, contemporary, and majorette technique. When she landed a job at San Diego State University (SDSU) several years later, June closed her Atlanta studio and reopened it in the new city, expanding her training ground to West Coast dancers.

Although June’s role as a coach and choreographer shifted her more behind the scenes, it still allowed her to stay connected to dance and continue to express her creativity.

“A dancer does the motion, and the choreographer creates the motion, so that’s always fun trying to find new and exciting ways to keep people interested in watching somebody move,” she says.

June also lent her choreography expertise to larger-scale projects, collaborating with the TV network VH1; rapper and singer Saweetie; and Fenty Beauty, Rihanna’s cosmetics brand, to create original content.

June’s approach to coaching stems from the belief that greatness is born from discipline and tough love. “Coach Bri,” as her dancers call her, finds the most rewarding part of her mentor role in seeing her dancers evolve, not just in their technique, but also in their character.

That evolution often begins with tryouts where June intentionally “shakes the tree” to see who is serious about dancing. The ones who make the team—both those who are already resilient and those who quickly learn to build thick skin—must then face “cuts,” meaning they have to earn their spots for specific performances.

While the goal is to get everyone to push their dancing to the next level, the competitive spirit June likes to foster is meant to be healthy: a dancer can miss out on a spot, congratulate the teammate who got it, and come back determined to earn the spot next time.

“You’re going to compete in life all the time, whether it’s for a job, for a promotion, whether it’s unconsciously, subconsciously,” June tells her dancers, “but it doesn’t have to be ugly. You can just put it all out there, do your best, then move on.”

The results of June’s coaching philosophy speak for themselves. Both her Atlanta and San Diego teams won multiple regional and national competitions. While at SDSU, she coached the SDSU Diamonds, the university’s dance team that became popular for their high-energy performances during athletic games. Today, many of June’s former dancers are professional backup dancers, NFL cheerleaders, or have become coaches and choreographers themselves.

For June, these examples illustrate how success is more than just trophies or titles; they show that her dancers have embodied the core values of putting in the work and loving what they do.

While June has only been at UOG for half a year, she is already making big moves. She is finding ways to motivate students to attend UOG and earn their degrees, but also to enjoy their college experience. Part of that plan has been establishing the Triton Spirit Squad, a student team that uses a fusion of dance and cheerleading to boost campus engagement and school spirit.

Beyond getting students involved in extracurriculars, June’s work is rooted in giving them the kind of support she remembers receiving from academic mentors during her own college days.

“That’s what drew me to both dancing and education, being that example for others,” she shares.

The opportunities to encourage young people remain plentiful for June. Whether she is guiding Tritons as they navigate their college plans or challenging her Spirit Squad members to find their rhythm, June is all about helping students and dancers alike recognize what they are capable of and giving them someone they can look to along the way.
